articles.title_orig: Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
articles.title_zh: Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
articles.content_orig:
Ford just reached a critical milestone in the development of its Fathom electric truck. The company has started manufacturing low-cost lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery packs at its $3 billion BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, located a couple hours west of Detroit, in Marshall, MI. These are production-grade LFP batteries which will first be used in Fathom prototypes before full-scale manufacturing begins next year.
One can’t overstate how important the Marshall plant is for Ford . It’s the first plant in the U.S. to manufacture LFP batteries for mainstream consumer vehicle use domestically. LG Energy Solution also produces LFP batteries in the U.S.—supplying to GM and Tesla —but they’re dedicated to stationary energy storage systems. Ford’s 2 million-square-foot facility is dedicated to automotive LFP batteries.
It has an annual production capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours and can manufacture 50 battery packs every hour. It’s a vertically integrated plant, where materials like raw lithium and iron-phosphate powder go in one end, and fully assembled, ready-to-install battery packs come out the other. All anode and cathode production, as well as major production processes in between, happen inside the plant.
Alan Clarke, the vice president of advanced development projects at Ford, said the company is moving fast to bring the Fathom to the market. In a relatively short time period, he claimed, Ford had developed the all-new Universal EV Platform that will underpin its future EVs, an all-new production system at the Louisville Assembly Plant, and domestic LFP battery production.
“Not having a team that existed to have a battery factory, a unicasting factory, an entirely new most automated vehicle production facility that Ford's ever produced in less than five years would be I think faster than China speed,” Clarke said during a media roundtable at the BlueOval Battery Park Michigan on Tuesday.
Clarke previously worked at Tesla for 12 years, helping create the Model S , followed by development work for the Model X , Model Y , Model 3 , and Cybertruck .
BlueOval Battery Park Michigan drone photo
I toured Ford’s LFP plant this week, and I think it’s one of the most advanced, highly-automated battery facilities in the U.S. Michigan, America’s automotive manufacturing hub for a century, certainly hasn’t seen anything like it in its history.
Part of the reason why the facility is so cutting-edge comes from Ford’s LFP licensing deal with China’s CATL, the world’s largest and the most advanced battery maker. The U.S. has been lagging behind China and Europe in the battery technology race. Ford is now bringing that technical know-how back to the U.S. even if that means licensing technology from CATL.
More importantly, Ford officials said the new plant is fully compliant with the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) rules. Raw materials used to make batteries here do not come from what the U.S. government designates as Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC). Even though the technology is from CATL, the critical materials aren’t sourced from U.S. FEOCs such as China, Russia and North Korea. (China controls the vast majority of the global critical materials supply chain.)
Final inspection of the Ford Fathom's LFP prismatic cells.
The plant is fully owned and operated by Ford, but CATL engineers helped the company set up thousands of incredibly complex production tools. They’re also helping train workers to operate high-tech equipment and install tight quality control systems to help Ford deliver the affordable EV that it has long promised. The prismatic LFP cell itself is unique to Ford and not something that exists in CATL’s global portfolio.
Meng Wang, the director and chief engineer of battery cell industrialization at Ford summed up the CATL partnership well. “To shorten our time to market, we decided to learn from the best,” Wang said. “Throughout the process, CATL passed on critical knowledge to Ford, including the equipment functions, manufacturing process, and also quality controls.”
Preorders for the Ford Fathom will begin early 2027 and production and deliveries are expected to begin by the end of next year.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin live: Leaders speak at APEC plenary ahead of unprecedented trilateral summit
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin live: Leaders speak at APEC plenary ahead of unprecedented trilateral summit
articles.content_orig:
President Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts are in China for a summit and a set of rare face-to-face talks between the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries.
Chinese President Xi Jinping and Mr. Trump addressed members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen. Mr. Trump said the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.
The president also vowed to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.
"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."
During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.
Mr. Trump and Xi are scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin next.
The U.S. president has said he's planning to discuss denuclearization with the leaders of China and Russia — which, along with the United States, make up the world's three largest holders of nuclear weapons.
But a range of other global challenges and points of tension are lingering in the background.
The summit is taking place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang , whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."
Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed , is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.
Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.
Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.
Iran is another contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.
The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."
Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island , which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."
And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported . Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

articles.title_orig: Trump pushes for three-way nuclear deal as Russia and China show little interest
articles.title_zh: Trump pushes for three-way nuclear deal as Russia and China show little interest
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has repeatedly placed nonproliferation near the top of the agenda for his trilateral meeting Thursday with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin , although his counterparts have expressed little interest in committing to new limitations on their nuclear arsenals.
Trump has been pushing for China to join the U.S. and Russia in a new nuclear arms control agreement since his first term in office. Still, he has sought to limit expectations for any major progress in Shenzhen, China, where the world’s top three nuclear powers are meeting on the sidelines of a summit of Asia-Pacific leaders .
Russia suspended its participation in New START, its last remaining nuclear arms pact with the U.S., when it invaded Ukraine in 2022, denying inspections of its nuclear sites. Ahead of the treaty’s expiration this past February , Russia said it would keep to the deal’s limitations on its arsenal for another year, but Trump insisted a new agreement must include China and possibly other nuclear powers.
China has said an arms control agreement should remain between the U.S. and Russia, which together hold nearly 90% of the world’s nuclear arsenal with more than 5,000 warheads each. China has about 600, according to Pentagon estimates, though by 2030 it could have up to 1,000 if its arsenal continues to expand at the current rate.
“China is building up its nuclear arsenal to a very significant degree, and it will continue to do so, and wants to continue to do so,” David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations, told reporters Wednesday.
The Chinese foreign ministry has declined to say whether nuclear arms control will be discussed at the trilateral meeting on Thursday, with spokesperson Mao Ning saying earlier this week that the three leaders “will have an in-depth exchange of views on important issues bearing on global peace.”
In a call last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi “agreed on the importance of meaningful leader-level conversations to advance goals such as peace and denuclearization,” according to a U.S. readout of the call. The Chinese readout made no reference to such a discussion.
Trump has admitted that it will be difficult to get Russia and China to consider reducing their nuclear arsenals.
“So we’re going to talk about denuclearization. Tough subject because it’s very hard for any of us to say we’ll get rid of our nukes, right? But especially since you do have other countries,” he said Monday. “But we’re going to be talking about denuclearization.”
Even in the hours leading up to this week’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, the world’s top two nuclear powers were making shows of force. On Tuesday, the U.S. launched an unarmed intercontinental ballistic missile in a previously unannounced test at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California. Hours later, Russia landed two strategic bombers in Vietnam to coincide with Putin’s arrival in China.
While one meeting is not likely to produce dramatic breakthroughs, it could kickstart a process that leads to sustained, formal bilateral or multilateral negotiations on nuclear risk reduction, arms control and disarmament, said Daryl Kimball, executive director of the Washington-based Arms Control Association.
“A top priority for all three leaders should be to head off a costly, escalatory nuclear arms race involving the further buildup of nuclear forces and the resumption of nuclear testing by any state,” he said.
Da Wei, director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University in Beijing, said nuclear arms control was not a “proper topic” for the trilateral meeting given the complexity of the issue and how little time Trump, Putin and Xi will have together.
But if the three leaders “can say something about nuclear stability, like a nuclear war is not winnable and should not be fought, I think that will be helpful,” he said in an interview Wednesday.
Rubio has acknowledged that a new agreement could take some time.
“Past agreements, including New START, took years to negotiate and were built upon decades of precedent. They were also between two powers, not three or more,” he wrote on Substack in February. “However, just because something is hard does not mean we should not pursue it or settle for less.”
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: Putin touts Russia’s economy at APEC as Ukraine sends it toward a fuel crisis
articles.title_zh: Putin touts Russia’s economy at APEC as Ukraine sends it toward a fuel crisis
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump shakes hand with Russian President Vladimir Putin, with Chinese President Xi Jinping also present, as leaders meet at the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026.
President Donald Trump met his Russian and Chinese counterparts, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, on Wednesday ahead of key talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen.
Trump touched down in the southern Chinese city Wednesday afternoon local time and was greeted by Xi on the runway, which is a notable departure from standard protocol. The two hugged and shook hands before heading to a banquet for the summit where all three leaders met informally ahead of sit-down talks Thursday.
At the banquet, Putin delivered remarks condemning European sanctions on Moscow, which have been in effect since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
“Artificial barriers at one level of the value chain lead to costs across all other links,” said Putin at the banquet, pointing toward European sanctions in particular, which he said have cut off “cheap and stable supplies of Russian energy resources” to Europe.
As a result, Putin claimed that the Eurozone was experiencing a “humiliating decline,” with energy sanctions placing a “heavy burden on European businesses and citizens, whose living standards are steadily declining.”
He also claimed that he would expect “significant potential benefits” from meeting the other leaders.
On Monday, the European Union announced plans to present its latest sanctions package, which Foreign Affairs Chief Kaja Kallas said will cover Russian refineries, banks, e-commerce, and any firms supporting Russia’s shadow fleet, a network of vessels that have helped transport Russian energy in attempt to circumvent sanctions.
Notably, Putin did not mention any U.S. sanctions currently in place on Russia during his plea to bring down international barriers on goods and trade.
In September, Congress passed a bill to introduce further sanctions on Moscow that would offer Trump the ability to enforce wide ranging tariffs on Russia and top countries that continue to purchase Russian energy, prompting concern among Democrat lawmakers as to the impact further tariffs could have on the American consumer .
Trump then signed an Executive Order in October, waiving many of the sanctions included in the bill and undercutting the additional pressure that new measures were intended to apply.
In his remarks at the APEC welcome banquet, Xi emphasized his focus on reducing trade restrictions. The Chinese President called on leaders to “remove trade and investment barriers to build an open Asia-Pacific economy.”
Many global trading partners have seen their relationship with the U.S. defined by tariffs since Trump’s return to Office, first seen in his "Liberation Day" levies that were largely quashed by the Supreme Court in February.
Xi also called for more cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI). “We should boost innovation to drive growth. We should forge science, technology and innovation partnerships, deepen cooperation in the digital economy and AI,” he said.
China’s pursuit of deepening ties on AI comes amid the fallout of Jensen Huang’s dismissal as Nvidia CEO last week, following his confession of an affair with a woman reportedly being investigated as a Chinese spy.
Thursday will see major talks held between Xi, Putin, and Trump in Shenzhen. The three leaders are scheduled for a trilateral meeting at 2:30 p.m. local time ( 1:30 a.m. Eastern ). The Kremlin said these talks would last “no more than an hour.”
Trump is also reportedly holding a separate meeting with Putin, according to the Associated Press. It would be their first direct meeting since failed talks last year in Alaska, during which they were meant to discuss peace negotiations regarding Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said “it is unlikely there will be time or opportunity here to hold full-scale negotiations” in Shenzhen, according to Russian state media TASS .

articles.title_zh: DealBook Summit: Elon Musk Paints Himself as Political Moderate, Says He Is ‘Not MAGA’
articles.content_orig:

Jabin Botsford/The Washington Post via Getty Images
The billionaire’s comments came during an interview at the New York Times DealBook summit.
Elon Musk, who spent nearly half a billion dollars on Republican campaigns in the recent U.S. midterm elections, is now claiming he is “not MAGA” after a historic blue wave secured Democratic majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives.
“I’m not MAGA,” the Tesla and SpaceX CEO told attendees of the New York Times DealBook summit on Wednesday night in a video interview with journalist Andrew Ross Sorkin.
The remark came after Sorkin pressed Musk, speaking remotely from the AMEC Summit in China, over public comments and posts he has made about the issue of immigration. A July Guardian analysis found that the near-trillionaire made twice as many X posts on the subject race and immigration ahead of SpaceX’s initial public offering than he did about his company.
“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he continued. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
The claim marks an about-face for a man who has campaigned with President Donald Trump, worn MAGA hats, and openly called himself “dark gothic MAGA.” Musk was not just the largest individual donor in the 2026 election cycle but across all of U.S. history, according to the Washington Post .
Throughout the conversation, Musk attempted to paint himself as having a more moderate political agenda, saying that he believes D.C. trifectas are dangerous, and claiming that his actual goal was securing a narrow Republican majority in the Senate.
“I think I’m ideologically quite moderate,” he said, adding, “I don’t think I have any kind of extreme political views.”
Elsewhere in the interview, Musk expressed buyer’s remorse over his massive political spending in the 2026 cycle, saying, “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it.”
“Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he added.
Musk’s $446 million spending in the 2026 cycle came atop more than $240 million spent on Republican campaigns in the 2024 presidential election. In both cycles, GOP advertising frequently deployed anti-LGBTQ+ and specifically anti-transgender rhetoric in an attempt to turn out voters. That strategy proved far more successful electorally in 2024 than it did in 2026. Overall, Republicans spent an estimated $183 million on anti-trans advertising in the midterms ahead of widespread losses.
As the New York Times reported, Musk’s America PAC specifically focused in September on the issue of trans participation in sports to try to defeat Democratic Senate candidates James Talarico, Sherrod Brown, and Josh Turek, who were campaigning in Texas, Ohio, and Iowa, respectively. Talarico, Brown, and Turek all won their races.

articles.title_orig: Inside Ukraine’s Coalition of the Wobbling
articles.title_zh: Inside Ukraine’s Coalition of the Wobbling
articles.content_orig:
When Vladimir Putin posed for the cameras with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, it marked a rare moment of international acclaim for Russia’s ruler since he ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
By contrast, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will on Thursday find himself among a motley assembly of small and medium-seized countries, convened by two weak European leaders and a rookie without a mandate.
The so-called Coalition of the Willing, an alliance of more than 35 nations supporting Kyiv, will gather in Berlin to try to work out how to help Zelenskyy steer his nation through another winter of brutal Russian bombardment and freezing temperatures.
But some diplomats and officials among Ukraine’s allies worry that this group has suffered a lack of leadership and faltering momentum in recent months, and could be consigned to irrelevance by any deal Trump concocts with Putin.
Four European government officials told POLITICO that the political authority of the coalition’s co-chairs — France, Germany and the U.K. — is crucial for Ukraine’s success but also weaker than it has been in years. “The leadership is wobbly in France and Germany,” said one European official, who like others quoted in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “In the U.K., [new prime minister] Andy Burnham seems to be quite solid on Ukraine but he’s still finding his way, so we are waiting.”
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz barely clung onto his job this fall after a surge in support for far-right populists led to what he admitted was electoral “disaster” for his center-right Christian Democrats. Emmanuel Macron, the French president, is historically unpopular and faces a wipeout for his centrist allies amid a wave of support for another far-right leader, Marine Le Pen, at next year’s presidential election.
Only Burnham has a solid majority backing him in parliament — but he has generally sought to focus on domestic policy since taking over from Keir Starmer in July without winning a general election, and remains relatively untested on the world stage.
The Coalition of the Willing began life on March 2, 2025, a few days after Trump and his vice-president JD Vance unleashed a torrent of criticism at Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, for allegedly not being grateful enough to the U.S. for its support.
In the ornate surroundings of Lancaster House in London, which served as a filming location for Netflix series The Crown, Starmer told gathering of 18 leaders he would put British “boots on the ground and planes in the air” if necessary to secure any peace deal that emerged for Ukraine. Macron made similar military commitments.
In the year or so that followed, the number of countries in the grouping doubled and Merz formally came aboard as a co-chair of the format.
When Trump seemed on the brink of trying to force Ukraine to accept what Europeans regarded as a toxic peace plan a year ago, the coalition became a critical bulwark in Zelenskyy’s defenses, one EU diplomat said.
It meant Ukraine’s backers had concrete evidence to show Trump that Europeans were willing to put their own soldiers, equipment and money on the line to guarantee a peace deal. The hope was that this would mean any settlement would be fair.
But momentum on peace talks and meetings of the coalition faded and dwindled after the U.S. and Israel launched into a war with Iran in the spring. Thursday’s gathering will be the coalition’s first leaders’ meeting since August.
It coincides with the coalition’s first military exercise, held in Poland, where thousands of troops are currently rehearsing how they would maintain any potential peace in Ukraine, despite that prospect still remaining out of reach.
Burnham is a relative newcomer to the world stage, and was not expected to make foreign policy a central plank of his premiership in the way Starmer did.
He confounded that expectation to some extent by holding a flurry of meetings with world leaders upon gaining the keys to No. 10 and reopening a highly fractious debate on the future of the U.K.’s relationship with the EU.
Nonetheless, some close observers argue upheaval at the top of government inevitably meant a setback in the highest level of diplomacy. Ed Arnold of the British Foreign Policy Group said “momentum has been lost through a change of PM,” while one U.K. minister noted this was also true for the U.K.’s new defense secretary, Wes Streeting.
A British official strongly denied Burnham would have any less energy for the coalition format or for supporting Ukraine than his predecessor. He is “really focused” on sustaining British backing for Ukraine, the official said, pointing to recently announced sanctions and assistance in developing long-range missiles . “The importance of the coalition of the willing is not receding in any way,” the official added.
Burnham himself sought to dissolve the distinction between foreign and domestic policy, saying in a speech on Monday : “The world is so interconnected now that it is impossible to disentangle decisions taken in Moscow with what happens on the ground in [his constituency seat] Makerfield.”
The revival of the coalition leaders’ engagement comes amid a renewed push from Trump to get a peace deal agreed .
The chief objectives of the meeting on Thursday are to develop plans for robust and legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine, including a multinational military force to safeguard a ceasefire; to commit additional funding for Kyiv’s war effort over the next year; to provide military support — especially air defenses against jet-powered drones, and long range strike capabilities; and to coordinate views on the ongoing peace negotiations mediated by Trump’s team.
On Wednesday, the European Commission proposed a loan of €45 billion in extra financial support for Ukraine for 2027. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was looking for more contributions from countries outside the EU, adding: “We will discuss the proposal also with our partners in the coalition of the willing.”
Another question preoccupying officials and diplomats as they prepared for the Berlin meeting was whether Trump will support Putin’s demands for reshaping European security and NATO’s role on the continent as part of the Ukraine peace process.
Many European governments already worry about the U.S. pulling troops out of Europe and some fear Trump’s criticism of NATO members has weakened the alliance’s ability to deter Russian aggression.
With these concerns in mind, officials in Brussels and European capitals were keeping a close eye on the meetings between Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, southeastern China.
“The danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit [in China] to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force,” said Bronwen Maddox , director of the Chatham House think-tank in London. “Ukraine will be able to hold out, but only with European help.”
A German official said the outcome of the Ukraine war is expected to shape Europe’s security architecture for years to come, and this will also form part of the discussion in the group on Thursday. A French official said far from acceding to Putin’s demands, Paris wanted Ukraine to join an expanded NATO.
In Kyiv, Zelenskyy’s government is desperate for as much support as possible from its backers, particularly when it comes to F-16 fighter jets, air defenses and money. But the Ukrainians also appreciate that, with the transatlantic alliance now fractured thanks to Trump’s policies over the past two years, an imperfect group such as the Coalition of the Willing is better than nothing and may be as good as it gets.
“They are doing a lot for Ukraine in terms of their capabilities,” one senior Ukrainian official told POLITICO. “Burnham is a great guy, he makes a lot of right moves. We are very happy to work with him. Merz and Macron are doing everything they can too.

articles.title_orig: APEC live: Trump says US has been 'Pacific power for hundreds of years'
articles.title_zh: APEC live: Trump says US has been 'Pacific power for hundreds of years'
articles.content_orig:
Kremlin says Ukraine was the main topic at the Trump-Putin bilateral
U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping pose for a photo during a bilateral meeting in Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. © Reuters
SHENZHEN -- Chinese President Xi Jinping is hosting leaders including U.S. counterpart Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin at this year's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum, showcasing his own country's technological prowess against a backdrop of cold and hot conflicts.
The proceedings in the southern tech hub of Shenzhen kicked off with a CEO Summit of business leaders on Tuesday, to be followed by an Economic Leaders' Meeting beginning Wednesday. On the sidelines, Xi and Trump are expected to have their third summit of the year as they seek to manage a fraught superpower rivalry.
As the Ukraine war drags on and tensions with Iran simmer, all eyes are on a trilateral summit among Xi, Trump and Putin that the White House has said will happen on Thursday. This prospect has drawn comparisons to the Yalta conference among the U.S., U.K. and Soviet Union to discuss the fate of postwar Europe in 1945.
Before departing for Asia on Monday, Trump told reporters that he might meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in China, a surprise announcement that could become another focal point of his visit.
Nikkei Asia is on the ground in Shenzhen to cover the meetings.

Here are the latest developments (Shenzhen time):
2:57 p.m. The Trump-Xi bilateral summit has ended, CCTV says.
2:49 p.m. Meanwhile, Taiwan's defence ministry said that two Russian military Tu-95 aircraft flew to the island's east on Thursday after approaching from the south, and then exited to its northeast.
2:10 p.m. The Kremlin said the issue of Ukraine was the main topic at the Trump-Putin bilateral, Reuters reported, citing Russia's Tass news agency.
Trump had said that he plans discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi, and later with Xi and Putin in the bilateral.
2:06 p.m. Xi described China-U.S. relations as overall stable and improving and added he was willing to work with Trump to continue steering bilateral ties on the correct course.
"I remain committed to working with you," Xi said to Trump.
Trump also said he planned to discuss ending Ukraine war with Xi and Putin in the trilateral.
1:58 p.m. Trump said at the start of his bilateral meeting with Xi that the U.S.-China Board of Trade has brought balance to the relationship between the two countries and that they have split up tariffs in fair ways.
Trump added that he and Xi felt strongly that oil should flow through the Strait of Hormuz, where an Iranian blockade in response to U.S.-Israeli attacks on the Islamic Republic has restricted shipments and pushed up energy prices. The U.S. president said he will ask China to do more for American farmers, staunch supporters of the Republican party.
1:40 p.m. Trump and Xi pose in front of U.S. and Chinese flags for photos
1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.
12:43 p.m. Trump met with Putin on the sidelines of the APEC forum following the plenary leaders session. Their meeting comes ahead a bilateral between Trump and Xi and a trilateral among the three leaders.
"We've had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they'll come out of this," Trump told Putin.
1:30 p.m. Trump has arrived at the Kylin Villa, a lakeside resort in Shenzhen that will serve as the venue for his bilateral summit with Xi and the trilateral including Putin.
12:35 p.m. Elon Musk told an APEC organizer that he was a "super fan" of China, according to a social media post by Yuyuan Tiantian, an account affiliated with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
According to the post, the Tesla and SpaceX boss told Ren Hongbin, president of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, about his admiration for China's "magnificent buildings and natural landscapes" as well as its railway system.
Tesla will continue to increase production in China, Musk said, according to the post. He was photographed sitting in a room across Ren, wearing a black jacket, pants and shoes.
12:06 p.m. APEC plenary session ends
10:58 a.m. Putin tells his APEC counterparts that Russia contributes to regional energy security and that they can "always count on Moscow." He also invites all regional partners to use Russian logistics infrastructure.
10:39 a.m. Trump spoke about the U.S. economy and claimed his administration is taming inflation. He also said in his remarks that trade deals were forthcoming.
"The United States has been a Pacific power for hundreds of years, and we continue to work to promote growth and stability, sovereignty, prosperity, and peace throughout this region," he said.
Trump also said AI regulation needed to be carefully managed and opposed measures that would "stifle" the industry. "We won't allow that to happen," he said.
Trump said he looked forward to meeting with Xi and Putin later this afternoon. but did not elaborate. The trilateral will follow a two-way meeting between Xi and Trump, their third this year.
10:30 a.m. Putin is taking the opportunity presented by APEC to shore up ties with Asian partners. He and Vietnamese leader To Lam agreed to step up cooperation with "a focus on traditional and new energy, including nuclear power, wind power and gas-fired power," according to Vietnam's readout.
The statement also says they "underscored the importance of maintaining peace, security and stability, increasing dialogue and cooperation, and upholding the role of multilateralism, the United Nations and the fundamental principles of international law."
10:10 a.m. In his opening address, Xi called for cooperation on Al and supply chains. The Chinese president proposed building "four key pillars" for development in the Asia-Pacific: economy and trade, connectivity, innovation and development.
He said China will provide $20 million to support cooperation in areas such as digital technology and clean energy.
9:50 a.m. Xi has opened the leaders summit, with the visiting dignitaries gathered around circular tables in a large conference room under chandeliers. Moments before sitting down for the plenary session, they took a photo with Xi in the center, flanked by Putin and Trump. Takaichi was positioned in the back row to the side.
9:40 a.m. In an interview with Fox News, Trump said he spoke with Xi about artificial intelligence, and former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang only came up "briefly," Reuters reports.
"I haven't heard that she was a spy," Trump said, in reference to Huang's extramarital affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.
9:30 a.m. APEC leaders are gathering for the forum's main event, which begins with a "family photo" before they convene for the plenary session. Xi has urged his guests to pursue "concrete results" promoting economic openness and innovation, but time is limited. Attention in the afternoon will turn to the U.S.-China bilateral meeting and the highly anticipated Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral. There are reports that Trump will squeeze in a one-on-one meeting with Putin as well, although it is unclear how substantial that would be.

articles.title_orig: Musk says Jensen Huang is irreplaceable, regrets midterm spending
articles.title_zh: Musk says Jensen Huang is irreplaceable, regrets midterm spending
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk compared Jensen Huang 's departure from Nvidia to kicking Michael Jordan off a team on a winning streak, while also expressing regret over how much he spent on the U.S. midterms.
"You've got a winning streak ... and then you kick Michael Jordan off your team," Musk told Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times' DealBook Summit on Wednesday. He added, "Doesn't seem like a smart decision to me."
Huang resigned last week following pressure after disclosing an affair with a woman who reportedly was suspected of being a Chinese spy, alongside reports of relationships with employees. He is expected to testify before the U.S. Congress next month around national-security and export-control issues.
The SpaceX and Tesla chief executive, who previously said it would be an "honor" to hire the Nvidia co-founder, added that no one could really replace Huang.
Musk said he had heard similar views about Huang's departure from Nvidia, including from President Donald Trump .
"I think the president has voiced publicly that he thinks Jensen should have stayed as CEO, and everyone I know thinks the same ... this is, at the end of the day, the Nvidia board decision," he said, adding, "We're not on the board, right?"
Musk and Huang have known each other for years through Nvidia's work with Tesla and OpenAI. Tesla has been a major Nvidia customer, while Huang has repeatedly praised Musk's AI strategy, including Tesla's self-driving work, xAI and the Optimus robot.
Asked about the midterms, Musk said he felt "pretty foolish" about spending at least $474 million with little to show for it, though he added that "maybe it would have been much worse without that."
Musk said his goal had been to prevent the presidency, House and Senate from all being controlled by one party. "If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money," he said.
In the same interview, he also appeared to distance himself from the MAGA movement. "I'm not MAGA," he said, adding that he wasn't sure what the term means.
On a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger, Musk said areas of overlap now exist that "didn't exist before," pointing to AI, robotics and the AI software and chip-design teams at both companies.
He said any deal would require shareholder approval and "may or may not succeed." Musk added that he could not push through a transaction that was bad for shareholders because he would "obviously get sued."
Asked whether he should receive his Tesla pay award if a merger were completed, Musk said he should not be rewarded "just for doing a merger" and should receive stock-option awards only if Tesla meets its performance targets.
Musk also said SpaceX rents computing capacity to Anthropic under short-term agreements that either side can terminate, adding that the Claude AI chatbot-maker had expressed interest in an additional 10 gigawatts.
Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share on Wednesday, raising $81.3 billion in what it said was the largest public offering on record, surpassing SpaceX.
Asked how he feels a year after describing his mind as "a storm," Musk said he feels "relatively at peace."

The US has carried out further strikes on Iran’s Qeshm ‌Island, despite Donald Trump ’s claim that the war is “effectively over”.
A fighter ⁠aircraft ‌targeted a missile launch site ‌on the island - situated along the Strait of Hormuz - after Iran previously struck American personnel and assets in Bahrain , Reuters reported, citing US officials.
The move was described by a global security expert as an attempt by the US to “degrade Iran’s capacity to threaten maritime traffic”.
Tehran on Wednesday retaliated to US strikes on Qeshm by launching air attacks on Bahrain and Kuwait , the defence ministries of the two Arab nations said.
It was Iran’s third strike on American military targets in Bahrain in five days, as tensions in the region continue to rise after more than nine months of confict.
Qeshm is Iran’s largest island and the largest in the Gulf, covering approximately 1,500 square kilometres. It stretches along the northern Strait of Hormuz, which connects the Gulf with the Gulf of Oman.
The island has 148,000 residents, primarily Sunni Muslims who speak the Bandari dialect.
In peacetime, the island is a tourist destination dotted with salt caves and the remnants of fortifications installed by European empires.
The Royal Indian Navy operated out of the island until 1863, and the last coaling station for the navy was abandoned in 1935 at the request of the Shah of Iran.
Since then, Iran has reconstituted the island with missiles, drones and fast-attack boats, giving it strategic importance for control of the Strait of Hormuz.
The island’s geographical location makes it one of the most vital pieces of territory for Tehran’s ability to control transit in the Strait of Hormuz.
Situated around 22 kilometres south of Bandar Abbas - Iran’s primary southern maritime, economic, and military gateway - and near the western and central approaches to the Strait of Hormuz, Qeshm gives Iran a critical viewpoint to track activity in the surrounding waters, particularly as it sits opposite the UAE, Omar and shipping routes serving the Gulf.
At the height of the US-Iran war, Qeshm was briefed as a possible target for a US ground offensive as Washington looked at ways to break Tehran’s hold on the Strait of Hormuz.
Exact details are kept confidential, but retired Lebanese Brigadier-General Hassan Jouni, a military and strategic expert, told Al Jazeera previously that the island has the ability to strike from an underground “missile city”.
Arman Mahmoudian, research fellow at the Global & National Security Institute at the University gf South Florida, told The Independent : “The recent American strikes against military facilities on Qeshm illustrate the island’s importance in the ongoing confrontation. Washington’s apparent objective is to degrade Iran’s capacity to threaten maritime traffic and American military assets.
“However, damaging military installations on Qeshm would not necessarily eliminate Iran’s ability to disrupt shipping, given the geographical dispersion of Iranian military capabilities along the coastline and across neighboring islands.
“Ultimately, Qeshm’s strategic significance lies not simply in Iran’s ability to control a particular piece of territory, but in its ability to use that territory to influence the security and economic calculations of other countries.
“For Tehran, Qeshm is not merely an island guarding the Strait of Hormuz; it is a strategic instrument through which Iran can transform its geographical position into military deterrence, economic leverage, and influence over the Persian Gulf.”
According to Can Kasapoğlu, a defence analyst, satellite imagery suggests Iran has installed a “significant portion of its anti-ship missiles in underground launch positions on Qeshm”.
He wrote for the Hudson Institute , a conservative think tank based in Washington, that “any US campaign in the region would likely centre on two decisive islands: Kharg and Qeshm”.
Rashid Al-Mohanadi, vice-president of Centre of International Policy Research and an expert in Gulf security, told The Telegraph that “Qeshm is likely to have the whole shebang” prepared for a possible invasion.
“Of course the island would have anti-ship capabilities, the coast is likely mined, the beaches booby-trapped and so on,” he said, adding that an additional threat would come from Iran’s ability to launch strikes from the mainland.
Overnight on Wednesday, a fighter ⁠aircraft ‌targeted a missile launch site ‌on Qeshm ‌Island.
The attack came after Iran previously struck American personnel and assets in Bahrain.
In June this year, the US military attacked a ground control tower on Qeshm in “self-defence”, claiming Iran had tried and failed to attack Kuwait and Bahrain with missiles.

articles.title_orig: Costco sees surge in emergency supply purchases amid tech outages
articles.title_zh: Costco sees surge in emergency supply purchases amid tech outages
articles.content_orig:
Consumers are panic-buying at Costco, snapping up generators and other emergency-preparedness items in response to a recent string of technology outages , according to investment firm Mizuho Securities.
"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report.
Shoppers are "pantry-loading," while 21 of the retailer's 26 "high-ticket generators" were sold out online as of Sunday night, he added.
The recent outages, which blocked access to Microsoft apps , snarled flights nationwide and hindered banking activities at various times during the past week, are raising questions among Americans about a larger cybersecurity threat, CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman said on "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday.
The companies affected by the outages have said they were due to issues such as routine maintenance or upgrades, while the Federal Aviation Administration blamed its nationwide ground stop last week on a contractor updating its flight system.
"All of them have denied that cyberattacks are to blame," Gutman said. "Still, the system failures are fueling online speculation about a larger cyber threat."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that there's "zero evidence" that the recent outages in the U.S. are linked.
"The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA . The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said during a news conference in the Philippines.
Costco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.
The close timing of the outages highlights the country's increasing reliance on technology, John D'Arcy, a Temple University professor who researches cybersecurity and information technology failures, told CBS News Philadelphia.
"Our systems are so much more complex and so much more interconnected than they ever have been in the past, that when we just have one failure, the effects are much more dramatic," D'Arcy said.
The surge in panic buying could lift Costco's sales, Bellinger wrote. He raised his target price for the company's stock to $1,150 from $1,100. Other big-box stores, including Walmart and Sam's Club, could see similar "pantry-loading lifts," he added.

articles.title_orig: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
articles.title_zh: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5tn (£1.14tn) as its shares are set to start trading on the stock market on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.
That will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.
Anthropic's stock market debut will make it the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public. It will also mark a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge amounts of money being poured into the technology will be profitable.
The firm said earlier this month it would offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.
But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.
The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.
If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.
Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.
However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price .
As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.
The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June .
OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.
Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.
There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.
Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.
"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.
While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.
"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.
Anthropic was started by a group of co-founders , led by siblings Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, all of whom left their work at OpenAI to start a new AI firm.
The company has carved itself out in the ongoing AI race as more focused on building the technology with safety top of mind.
It refused to comply with a demand by the US Department of Defense that Anthropic's tools be used in an essentially unrestricted way.
CEO Dario Amodei has been outspoken in his belief that AI tools may soon be so powerful that they present a threat to human existence.
The company has urged developers to slow the development of AI, arguing that advanced systems could pose "catastrophic" risks to humanity if they are not handled with appropriate safeguards.
Rival firm OpenAI has also voiced similar concerns about the technology's risks and delayed its plans to list on the stock market to address AI safety concerns.
Nonetheless, Anthropic is looking to grow quickly and gain more access to financing through the public markets in order to do so.
Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.
"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."
But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.
The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.
A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

articles.title_orig: The Jensen Huang Saga Has Reinvigorated Washington’s China Hawks
articles.title_zh: The Jensen Huang Saga Has Reinvigorated Washington’s China Hawks
articles.content_orig:
This week, the Trump administration made it significantly harder for Chinese companies to access some of the world’s most advanced AI chips. For years, tech firms like Alibaba and ByteDance could rent computing power from data centers overseas, allowing them to use powerful Nvidia chips they were generally prohibited from physically importing into China . This is known as remote access.
But under new plans announced on Monday, overseas data centers that want to provide large amounts of computing power to China will have to get special licenses and deal with other annoying new kinds of red tape. The White House also imposed stricter rules on shipments of advanced chips to five countries, including Singapore and Malaysia, where US officials suspect significant levels of smuggling may have taken place.
These are not new policy ideas, and similar proposals have been kicking around in Washington for a while. But the timing of Monday’s announcement is impossible to ignore. Yes, this is about Jensen Huang’s sex life.
As you’ve probably heard by now, the Nvidia cofounder resigned as CEO last week after admitting he had an affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. Alice previously worked at the Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which offered remote access services and is suspected of engaging in chip smuggling.
The scandal may have been so embarrassing for the White House that officials felt compelled to demonstrate they had the situation under control. Apparently, the cheating scandal of the century was the motivation they were missing. (A White House spokesperson previously told WIRED that the new rule would “crack down on the smuggling of advanced US SI chips” and “help ensure that America’s most advanced chips go first to US SI innovators, not Chinese shell companies.”)
It started in the fall of 2022, when the Biden administration unveiled a set of rules that would radically alter the future of AI and who was allowed to build it. The goal was to choke off China's access to the advanced chips needed to train the world's most powerful AI models, as well as the equipment required to manufacture those chips.
It's worth remembering just how radical this approach was at the time. For decades, the US had used export controls to keep sensitive American technology away from specific military programs, governments, and blacklisted companies accused of carrying out human rights abuses. But the Biden administration was attempting something far more ambitious: using Washington's influence over the global semiconductor industry to hold back the world's second-largest economy from competing at the cutting edge of one of the most important new technologies in generations.
The strategy rested on a relatively simple idea. Training the most advanced AI models requires enormous amounts of computing power, and American companies like Nvidia dominate the market for the chips that provide it. By restricting China's access to those chips, Washington hoped to preserve America's technological lead.
Four years later, the US certainly cannot claim total victory. But boy, have things gotten messy. Part of the problem is that Washington tasked the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), a relatively small, underfunded agency within the Commerce Department, with leading enforcement of the controls. The bureau had a budget of just $235 million in 2026—a paltry sum compared to what Nvidia rakes in in a single week.
The bureau's job only got harder as the Biden administration introduced successive rounds of increasingly complex restrictions, scrambling to tighten the rules as chipmakers found increasingly elaborate ways to get around them. But one of the bureau's biggest challenges was fighting what became a booming industry for smuggling AI chips into China.
At BIS, Megaspeed has become a poster child for the problem, although it's far from the only company suspected of involvement, or even the largest, according to a person familiar with the matter.
According to Bloomberg, roughly 50,000 of the estimated 136,000 AI chips Megaspeed imported into Malaysia and Indonesia in 2024 and 2025 weren't accounted for in Nvidia's initial inventory checks. It's not clear where they may have ended up. (Nvidia later said it had found at least some of them.)
Even if all of the unaccounted-for chips ended up in China, they would represent only a fraction of the advanced semiconductors believed to have been smuggled into the country over the past few years. Researchers at the Institute for Progress estimate that, by the end of 2026, China could have accumulated smuggled computing power equivalent to roughly 1 million of Nvidia's high-end H100 chips.
But all along, Chinese companies didn't necessarily need to smuggle chips into the country to use them. They could just rent computing power from data centers in other countries, and best of all, the practice didn’t violate US export controls. This wasn’t some hidden loophole—every policymaker and researcher who worked on the chip restrictions was deeply aware of it. So why let the practice continue?
For one, renting computing power can be more expensive and cumbersome than owning the chips outright, especially for companies that need to train large AI models over long periods. Some analysts argued that allowing Chinese firms to use American technology overseas could help keep them dependent on it instead of pushing them to develop domestic alternatives. Restricting access would also be difficult to enforce and could hurt US technology companies.
Now, Washington is moving into this territory anyway. Monday's announcement represents another significant expansion of US efforts to control China's technological development. In 2022, Washington set out to prevent Chinese companies from acquiring certain American chips. Four years later, it’s trying to regulate how Chinese companies use those same chips, even when the hardware never enters China.
Whether that's a good idea depends partly on how much the original restrictions have actually accomplished.
There is evidence that export controls have made it considerably harder for Chinese AI companies to acquire the kind of computing power of their American competitors. But assessing the precise impact of the policies has proven to be extremely difficult.
This strategy comes with a lot of risks, and like with everything else in life, there are real winners and losers. For example, forcing US chip companies to cut off Chinese customers has come at a cost to American companies. In a study of earlier US export restrictions , researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York found that affected American suppliers struggled to replace lost business in China with new customers elsewhere. They estimate that the restrictions wiped $130 billion from the companies’ combined market value, while also hurting their profitability and employment.
The restrictions have also given China a very powerful incentive to find ways to compete in AI without relying on American technology. Huawei, for example, developed a way to link powerful chips together to create larger, more powerful megachip systems. The Chinese AI lab DeepSeek proved to the world that finding ways to make training more efficient could help developers build competitive models with fewer resources.
I worry that the Trump administration will soon find that it has gotten out over its own skis. It’s now trying to control not only which chips Chinese companies can buy from American companies, but also how they can use American technology anywhere it may be in the world. I’m not sure that is the kind of responsibility I want to bestow on anyone in response to what happened in one person’s sex life.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia is offering engineers more money. That may not be enough to keep them.
articles.title_zh: Nvidia is offering engineers more money. That may not be enough to keep them.
articles.content_orig:
Before Nvidia's earnings call this week, Ben Reitzes, a top tech analyst at Melius Research, laid out what interim leadership needs to do to steady the ship following Jensen Huang 's ouster.
At the top of his list was keeping Nvidia's engineers from leaving.
"What's the go-forward plan there of retaining all the engineers?" Reitzes told investors in a video. "The road map, in our opinion, is actually the most important for a long-term investor. Can they keep it on track? What are they doing to retain the talent to keep it on track?"
It's a crucial question for Nvidia, which has lost about $500 billion in market value since its board ousted Huang last week, sparking an extraordinary backlash from some employees, investors, and other technology leaders.
Nvidia risks losing some of the engineers responsible for creating the chips and other highly technical systems that have made it the world's dominant AI hardware company.
Technical talent is especially important in Silicon Valley because the products companies sell can change dramatically from one generation to the next.
Compare that to a bank. Its core business involves accepting deposits, making loans, and managing investments. While leadership matters, the products are well established, and experienced executives can generally take over without having to reinvent them.
Technology companies face a different challenge. Their success often depends on developing products that don't yet exist, anticipating what customers will need years in advance, and making technical decisions that competitors struggle to replicate. One mistake and a new wave of invention can wipe you out.
That requires more than good management. It takes engineers with unusual skills, working under leaders who understand the technology well enough to recognize which ideas are worth pursuing — years before they materialize.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Huang combined those qualities at Nvidia. He helped turn a maker of graphics chips for video games into the company supplying much of the computing power behind the AI boom.
His ouster raises questions about whether Nvidia can preserve that combination of technical expertise, leadership, and long-term vision.
"A concentrated product brings concentrated risk," Christopher Brown, an investment professional at Synovus, told Business Insider.
Nvidia is especially dependent on a closely connected collection of chips, software, and other technology that powers its AI business. Losing the people responsible for developing those products could therefore have an outsize impact, Brown said.
Brad Gastwirth, head of research at Circular Technology, said the departure of just a handful of senior engineers could cause serious problems.
"Losing even five to 10 critical technical leaders could have a disproportionate impact, particularly if those individuals are responsible for architectural decisions or coordinating major product transitions," he told Business Insider.
Nvidia's competitors have plenty of reasons to take advantage of the turmoil.
"I would absolutely expect competitors, including AMD, Broadcom, hyperscalers and AI startups, to aggressively recruit Nvidia engineers," Gastwirth said.
Brown agreed, describing efforts to recruit Nvidia technical talent as inevitable.
"His team loves him. And many of them are there because of him, and have had higher offers to go elsewhere and have turned them down because of personal loyalty to Jensen," Elon Musk said following Huang's departure.
On Tuesday, Huang said he'd be honored to return as CEO if the board approves. He cited support from a wide range of constituents, and at the top of his list were Nvidia employees.
"I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO," Huang said in a statement .
Thousands of Nvidia employees have signed an open letter calling for Huang's reinstatement, while some have publicly criticized the decision to oust him.
"I'm deeply disappointed in our board," Nvidia research scientist Shang-Wen Li wrote on X on Wednesday.
Darrell Dai , a Nvidia robotics researcher who resigned following Huang's ouster, praised the former CEO's willingness to invest in technologies before their commercial potential became obvious.
Dai also highlighted the working environment Huang created.
"Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes," he wrote.
Nvidia's interim CEO, Colette Kress , is trying to address the retention threat.
At an Nvidia all-hands meeting Wednesday, Kress told employees that pay raises and additional stock grants would arrive in December, earlier than originally planned.
The company also sought to reassure staff that its technology plans and relationships with customers remained intact.
Even though Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, is widely respected on Wall Street, her background lacks the technical experience essential to shaping Nvidia's products over the next decade.
The board is searching for a permanent CEO replacement, considering both internal and external candidates.
In the meantime, money could help Nvidia retain engineers.
One employee who attended Wednesday's all-hands meeting told Business Insider that better compensation is an attractive short-term incentive. The person questioned whether it would be enough over the longer term.
They said that with the stock having already exploded over the past decade, the added compensation may not be a sufficient motivation.
Indeed, Nvidia's extraordinary stock performance has already made many longtime employees millionaires , giving some considerable financial freedom.
Gastwirth said the greater danger lies in what happens over the next several years, as Nvidia must make decisions about future generations of AI technology without the leader who helped establish its dominance.
"Jensen wasn't simply managing Nvidia," he said. "He had an extraordinary ability to anticipate where computing and AI were heading and position the company years ahead of competitors."
His departure could set off a chain reaction if other important technical leaders decide to leave, Gastwirth warned.
"Nvidia could lose not only critical engineering expertise but also some of the strategic thinking that has allowed it to consistently stay ahead of the industry," he said.

articles.title_zh: Stock Market News, November 18, 2026: Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors’ Nerves
articles.content_orig:
This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox.
Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today's edition of Morning Squawk.
Investors will have to divide their attention between a series of huge market events today.
President Trump is in China for a crucially timed summit between America, China and Russia, with the future of AI chip exports a key issue.
Nvidia shares look set to lift the Nasdaq after the group posted a solid set of earnings amid its leadership shake-up.
And Anthropic is expected to price its IPO in another record moment for markets.
President Donald Trump has arrived in Shenzhen , China, for an unprecedented trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin .
In a rare move, Xi met President Trump on the tarmac as Air Force One arrived, with CNBC's Sri Jegarajah reporting from Shenzhen that this is a symbolic act by the Chinese leader, sending a significant foreign policy message.
Ahead of the summit, set to take place tomorrow, all three leaders have laid out their priorities:
Nvidia shares are trading higher in premarket moves. Chipmaking peers, server stocks and neocloud firms are all trading higher alongside Nvidia.
The chipmaker appeared to brush aside its leadership turmoil to deliver another blockbuster quarter .
In an exclusive interview with Jim Cramer , interim CEO Colette Kress focused on the path ahead , despite the speculation around Huang's hopes to return, saying "the most important thing we have seen is growth in the demand that's out there."
During the "Mad Money" interview Tuesday evening, Kress emphasized that major customers have continued expressing interest in the company's products. "I have seen already with many of these [customers] contacting me and saying, 'Great to see everything intact. Great to see that there's more supply. I need more demand.'"
Sources have told CNBC that Anthropic will likely price above its current IPO range of $70-78. That's according to multiple people speaking to CNBC's David Faber.
CNBC's Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning.
Subscribe here to get access today .
A series of technology disruptions has raised concerns over cybersecurity and the vulnerability of certain systems.
Over recent days, outages have impacted Microsoft, the FAA, JPMorgan Chase transactions and Apple.
Speaking to CNBC on Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton dismissed suspicions that malicious activity, saying, "This is not cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state... We've looked very closely."
Democrat Mary Peltola wins Alaska Senate election
Democratic candidate Mary Peltola won the Alaska Senate election, capping a midterm cycle that already was one of the best for Democrats in more than a half-century, the Associated Press reported Tuesday evening.
Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in a race that was surrounded by controversy over an independent candidate who shared his name.
— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng, Anniek Bao, Kif Leswing, Tobias Burns, Alexa LoMonaco,  Fred Imbert, Ashley Capoot, Caleigh Keating and Dan Mangan contributed to this report.
Jack Sommers edited this edition.

articles.title_orig: Siri Modular Apple Watch face gains two new styles with watchOS 27.3
articles.title_zh: Siri Modular Apple Watch face gains two new styles with watchOS 27.3
articles.content_orig:
Siri Modular, the new Apple Watch face in watchOS 27, is gaining new style options. watchOS 27.3, currently in beta, adds two more style options to the existing set. This gives users five options for adjusting what type of information appears on Siri Modular.
Siri Modular originally shipped with three style options. Each supports a small line complication above the time.
Additionally, the original three styles include these options:
In watchOS 27.3, Apple introduces two new Siri features that work with Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 .
First, there’s Siri Recap which uses the Apple Watch to turn audio into high-level text summaries. Second, there’s Live Rewind which lets you view a transcript of the last 15 seconds of spoken word.
The two new Siri Modular Apple Watch face styles help surface three things: invoking Siri, viewing conversations with Siri, and viewing Siri Recaps on the Apple Watch.
The new styles include a pill-shaped module that includes icon shortcuts that go directly to Siri conversations, invoke Siri AI, or go directly to Siri Recaps in the Siri app.
One style features a large digital clock with the new three-button Siri module. Another includes a compact digital clock with a Smart Stack tile and the new three-button Siri module.
This brings the style options to five. If you use the three circular complications configuration, you can also assign a Siri icon that invokes Siri AI.
watchOS 27.3 is currently in beta and expected to be released officially in December.

articles.title_orig: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.title_zh: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
articles.content_orig:
It had been a year and a half since Ukraine last attacked the 19-kilometer-long Kerch Bridge connecting Russian-annexed Crimea with Russia's Krasnodar region.
Now, Ukraine has struck again. The attack during the night of November 17 caused the highway section of the bridge to collapse into the sea. As a result, shipping traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov has also been disrupted.
Russia's ministry of transport announced a "temporary suspension" of road and rail traffic on the bridge, though later, rail services were resumed. Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." It was only after this announcement that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed the attack.
The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula , an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.
It has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion . The most well-known strike occurred in October 2022, when an explosives-laden truck detonated on the bridge, causing extensive damage and several months of traffic restrictions. The most recent attack took place in June 2025, when the SBU reported that an underwater support structure was blown up.
The latest Ukrainian operation lasted about a month, and consisted of seven distinct phases. "First, the SBU and armed forces systematically neutralized the enemy's air defense system. After that, the direct attack on the bridge began," says the SBU Telegram channel.
Some Russian military bloggers claim that the attack was carried out with the support of Ukraine's Western allies, or at least using their equipment and weapons.
Ukraine has not confirmed this. It has instead pointed out that various Ukrainian-made weapons were used in the attack, ranging from a variety of drones, to FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptun missiles. British daily The Times has cited Ukrainian military sources, saying that Ukraine attacked the bridge without the support of SpaceX's satellite network system Starlink . There has been no confirmation of this so far.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , meanwhile, described the strike as a response to Russian attacks: "Russia is attacking our infrastructure every day, particularly bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region." He said "we are rebuilding our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that the war always returns to where it began."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
After the attack, pictures and videos of the bridge were shared on social media. The Krimskij Veter Telegram channel has highlighted damage to the railroad link and questioned why Russian authorities have opted to resume train services.
The Kerch Strait shipping channel is also completely blocked by debris. "This brings road traffic to a standstill, but also shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the channel writes.
Indeed, the Kerch Strait navigational channel is merely 120 meters wide, writes Mychajlo Hontschar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" on Facebook. "The strait is shallow, only three to five meters deep."
As early as the 19th century, the seabed was dredged to allow heavier ships to pass from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and vice versa. "Now, Vladimir Putin's bridge-building efforts have brought shipping to an indefinite standstill," Hontschar said.
Not only will river-sea vessels no longer be able to leave the waters of the Sea of Azov, the Don, and the Volga, but boats and small ships from the Black Sea fleet and the Caspian flotilla based in Novorossiysk will also be unable to do so.
Many pro-Kremlin Telegram channels have been quick to claim that the bridge does not play an important role in the Russian army's logistics or in supplying Crimea.
The Dva Mayora (Two Majors) channel quotes the "Deputy President of the Republic of Crimea," Olga Kurlayeva, who described the bridge as a "purely civilian structure."
Ukrainian military experts interviewed by DW, on the other hand, point to the systematic disruption of Russian logistics. These efforts also included regular attacks on the R-80 highway leading through Russian-occupied territories of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.
Russia cannot replace the Kerch Bridge with any other land connection, says Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military expert with the Information Resistance Group that seeks to counter disinformation. He expects the damaged bridge will cause supply problems for the Russian armed forces: "If there is a resource shortage during attacks or in defense, then either the attacks or the defense will fail."
That is why he does not rule out a decline in attacks from occupied Crimea on the rest of Ukraine. "There are many launch pads for kamikaze drones in Crimea — in the Hvardijsk area, at Cape Chauda and in Balaklava," Kovalenko told DW. "From there, many drones are launched toward Odesa, Mykolaiv, and the right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. They also fly over Crimea en route toward Ukraine. Then there are attacks using Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as Zircon and Oniks missiles, guided missiles, and glide bombs. And while they don't originate in Crimea, they are brought over via the Kerch Bridge."
Kovalenko says the bridge strike has dealt a serious blow to Vladimir Putin's standing. It comes at a sensitive time as Putin is about to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China .
Memes and witty comments about the bridge abound on X. Meanwhile, the Russian president's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has promised to rebuild the bridge and assured that it will be "even better than before."
Andrii Korezkyj of the Kyiv University of Transportation, however, says this is not likely to happen anytime soon. "All in all, I would estimate that it would take between one and a half and three years [to rebuild]," Korezkyj told DW, adding, "I don't think they'll let the Russians build another [bridge] arch like that near the Ukrainian border without interference."
Pro-Russian commentators, known as Z-bloggers, agree with this view. "Unlike in 2022 and 2023, the Ukrainian armed forces are now able to launch strikes against floating cranes and repair teams."
"Even installing a pre-assembled arch under these conditions would constitute a challenging task," writes the pro-Kremlin Rybar Telegram channel.
This article was translated from German.
